author: JILL ZIMA BORSKI
title: Marathon council votes to keep taxes flat - NewsBreak
text:
By JILL ZIMA BORSKI ,
9 hours ago
MARATHON — The Marathon City Council voted to keep property taxes flat during a Sept. 16 public hearing on the proposed 2025-2026 fiscal year millage rate and budget.
It was to finalize the budget and millage rate on Tuesday, Sept. 23, after press time.
The proposed 2025-2026 tentative millage rate was 2.2235 mills, which is $222.35 for every $100,000 of taxable property value. The tentative millage rate was equal to a 7.77% increase in total property taxes. The council, however, rejected that rate in favor of the rollback rate of 2.0631 ($206.31 per $100,000), which is the property tax rate that generates the same amount of revenue as the current fiscal year. The rollback rate passed unanimously.
The council was pleased to have achieved rollback rate for two consecutive years. The municipal calendar runs from Oct. 1, 2025, through Sept. 30, 2026.
In the coming year, the city is buying two new public works trucks and trading in one that will net about $6,900 to help offset a portion of the purchase amount, said City Manager George Garrett. The city also is instituting a new way to track maintenance service to the vehicles.
The council suggested budget reductions might be reaped from putting more contracts, such as sewer upgrades ,out to bid for the possibility of lower costs and reducing the amount of the city’s annual donations to nonprofit organizations.
Resident Mike Mallard questioned a few of the city’s costs, such as substantial retirement benefits in the fire-rescue department. Local chamber of commerce director Daniel Samess questioned $1.4 million in increased costs for the coming year and urged the council to seek ways to bring down costs, including using reserve funds if necessary. Another resident questioned earmarking the equivalent of 20% of the city manager's salary for his retirement fund.
“Where’s the oversight?” he asked. He added that the city’s charter mandates the council to find ways to increase revenues. “What’s being done about that?” he asked.
Moving on with the agenda, Garrett said the lobbying contract with Ballard Partners Inc. for services in Tallahassee is to come back to the council for approval in the coming months. The city hopes to secure a month-by-month payment agreement versus annual, he said.
The city next heard a request for a conditional use permit from a representative of Casa Manana, a 7.61-acre beachfront condominium offering residents access to the water and ocean views on Boca Chica Key. It is to offer a nature walk, hammock area, food truck and nine market rate units, according to the speaker. The permit was approved.
Master electrician Armand Messina, representing the Florida Keys Contractors Association, spoke to council about implementing a CU (competency units) program to help ensure professionalism in the contracting community. Messina thanked the city’s code enforcement for addressing unlicensed contractors.
On the city’s to-do list is seeking state and national grant funds for its mandated deepwater well for wastewater treatment. It’s a five-year plan and is required through a federal judgment order, said Garrett.
Libby Frazier, utilities deputy director, was recognized for service as she is celebrating 15 years with the city of Marathon.
